settings.content: Coloured stones, one at a time, with honest advice on what each can take

settings.heading: Chosen With the Heart as Much as the Eye
settings.body:
A coloured stone says something a diamond cannot. It signals personality, taste and choice: a stone selected for the wearer rather than for the wedding industry.

Coloured gemstones are described by three qualities of colour rather than the Four Cs. Hue is the colour family, tone is how light or dark it appears, and saturation is how vivid or muted it is. Strong, evenly distributed colour at a medium tone almost always looks more beautiful than a darker but patchy stone, and clarity standards are looser: most coloured stones contain visible inclusions, and that is entirely normal.

The most valuable colour is not always the best colour for the wearer. A dark sapphire may be technically impressive and still look heavy on the hand. Colour also shifts between daylight, office light and candlelight, which is why we always show stones in more than one light.

settings.heading: Eight Gemstone Guides
Platinum and White Gold
settings.body: Cooler and cleaner. White metals let a stone's own colour read accurately, and suit blues, greens and icy pastels.

settings.heading: Yellow Gold
settings.body: Warms a stone. Blues, greens and warm-toned stones feel richer against yellow gold, and it flatters antique cuts.

settings.heading: Rose Gold
settings.body: Softens pink, peach, champagne and purple tones. Morganite in rose gold is the most requested combination we make.

settings.intro: The same stone reads differently depending on what surrounds it. Choose the pairing, not just the stone.
settings.heading: The Metal Changes the Colour
Match the Stone to the Life It Will Lead
settings.body: Hardness resists scratching. Toughness resists chipping. They are different properties and the two are constantly confused, which is how people end up with an opal engagement ring they have to take off to do the washing up.
